It is called repainting. It is an inherit design of how a browser operates that is either abused or ignored.

When a site loads the initial content, your browser is given a list of other things to get. This usually includes images or other content/scripts to load after the initial page load is done. When the new content comes in, if the initial load didn't specify height and width of what would be coming in, then it adapts by repainting the site as soon as the browser knows the dimensions.

The abuse comes when your browser wants to load so many things at once but can only handle a limited amount at a time. JavaScript, for instance, can only be done two scripts at a time (I think). Your browser gets those two, scans through them and runs what it finds. Once it is all done with that, it gets the next two, and so on until all are complete. There are smart developers that will combine all the scripts into one so that a repaint happens once. Novice or those who don't know this tidbit, will list out up to a dozen or so scripts. That means multiple jumps, inciting rage among users.

There is something coming down the pipe for browsers called webworkers, which will address this problem. They will be a worker queue, each worker capable of downloading something for the page and loading it by taking advantage of [technical mumbo-jumbo]. Rather than two scripts at a time, they will get fired off as soon as your browser knows about them. This means if you have a decent enough computer, you probably won't even see any jumps from a repaint. All those calculations will happen fast enough so that it is all in the initial render. But that is still a few years off before wide adoption.
